                ok = Y[[a, b]].notna().all(axis=1)
                dy, dp = (Y[b] - Y[a])[ok].values, (P[b] - P[a])[ok].values
                r = float(np.corrcoef(dy, dp)[0, 1]) if dy.std() > 0 else float("nan")
                perm = [abs(np.corrcoef(rng.permutation(dy), dp)[0, 1]) for _ in range(2000)] if dy.std() > 0 else [1]
                dr[f"{g}|{b}-{a}"] = dict(r=r, p=float((np.sum(np.array(perm) >= abs(r)) + 1) / (len(perm) + 1)), n=int(ok.sum()),
                                          mean_dproj=float(dp.mean()))
                print(f"  dose-response {g:18s} {b}-{a}: mean dproj={dp.mean():+.2f} corr(dproj, dy)={r:+.3f} p={dr[f'{g}|{b}-{a}']['p']:.3f} n={ok.sum()}")
        out[m]["dose_response"] = dr
    prev = {}
    path = os.path.join(ROOT, "results", "steer_summary.json")
    if os.path.exists(path):
        prev = json.load(open(path))
    prev.update(out)
    json.dump(prev, open(path, "w"), indent=1)

    main()

Base directory for this skill: /tmp/claude-1000/bundled-skills/2.1.283/f8c2bb90daa08bfb53c364ee49b76807/dataviz

# Data Visualization

A chart is **read by people and executed by you**. This skill turns "make it look
good" into a procedure with checks, so the result is right by construction rather
than by taste.

**The method here is design-system-agnostic.** Nothing in the procedure, the form
heuristic, the six checks, or the mark specs is specific to one product. A design
system supplies a small set of *parameters* (its ramps, a categorical order, a
diverging pair, a status palette, a texture, its surfaces, its filter components);
the method consumes them unchanged. A **validated default palette** is the
reference instance, fully specified in `references/palette.md`. To target your
brand, read that file's structure and substitute its values - touch nothing else.

> The single most important habit: **the color part is computable, so compute it.**
> Never eyeball whether a palette is colorblind-safe - run `scripts/validate_palette.js`.

## The procedure - do these in order

Color comes LAST. Most bad charts pick colors first.

1. **Pick the form.** What is the data's job - magnitude, identity, polarity, a
   single headline, change-over-time? The job picks the chart type, and sometimes
   the answer is *not a chart* (a stat tile or hero number). -> `references/choosing-a-form.md`
2. **Assign color by the job it does.** Categorical (identity), sequential
   (magnitude), diverging (polarity), or status (state) - each has one rule.
   Assign categorical hues in fixed order, never cycled. -> `references/color-formula.md`
3. **VALIDATE the palette - run the script, don't reason about Delta E.**
   `node scripts/validate_palette.js "<hex,hex,...>" --mode light` (relative to
   this skill's base directory - or load it as `<script type="module">` in the
   chart's own page, where it reads
   `data-palette` off `<body>` and logs a `console.table` report). It returns
   pass/fail on the lightness band, chroma floor, adjacent-pair CVD separation,
   the normal-vision floor, and contrast. Fix anything that FAILs before continuing. Re-run for
   `--mode dark` with that mode's surface.
4. **Apply mark specs & spacers.** Thin marks, 4px rounded data-ends anchored to
   the baseline, 2px lines, >=8px markers, a 2px surface gap between fills (stacked
   segments and adjacent bars alike) and a 2px surface ring on overlapping marks,
   selective direct labels. -> `references/marks-and-anatomy.md`
5. **Add the hover layer - by default.** An HTML/SVG chart *is* interactive; ship
   a crosshair+tooltip on line/area and a per-mark hover tooltip on bar/dot/cell.
   The only form that skips it is a bare stat tile with no plot. Hit targets bigger
   than the mark; filters in one row above the charts. -> `references/interaction.md`
6. **Final accessibility pass.** For >= 2 series a legend is always present and <= 4
   are also direct-labeled (a single series needs no legend box - the title names
   it), so identity is never color-alone; a table view exists; dark mode is **selected** - its own
   steps from the same ramps, validated against the dark surface, not an automatic
   flip; texture is available for the CVD/print/forced-colors case.
7. **Render it and look at it.** The validator checks color, not layout - open or
   screenshot the output and eyeball it for label collisions, geometry, and overflow
   before calling it done.

Then check the result against **`references/anti-patterns.md`** - it is the catalog
of what goes wrong. If your chart matches an entry, it's wrong.

## Non-negotiables (true in every design system)

- **Assign categorical hues in fixed order, never cycled.** A 9th series is never a
  generated hue - it folds into "Other," small multiples, or composite encoding.
- **One axis.** Never a dual-axis chart (two y-scales). Two measures of different
  scale -> two charts, small multiples, or indexed to a common base. *(This is the
  #1 chart mistake - see anti-patterns.)*
- **Color follows the entity, never its rank.** A filter that changes the series
  count must not repaint the survivors.
- **Sequential = one hue, light->dark. Diverging = two hues + a neutral gray
  midpoint.** Never a rainbow; never a hue at the diverging midpoint.
- **Run the validator before shipping any categorical palette.** CVD Delta E >= 8 is the
  target (OKLab ×100); 6-8 is a floor that is legal ONLY with secondary encoding. A
  normal-vision floor below 15 is a hard FAIL - full-color readers can't tell the
  pair apart; re-step it on the adjacent pairlist (secondary encoding does not excuse
  this one); under `--pairs all` cut series or facet instead - see check 4. A contrast WARN
  obligates visible labels or a table view - it is not dismissable.
- **Thin marks; a legend always present for >= 2 series (none for one), with
  selective direct labels (never a number on every point); recessive grid/axes.**
- **Text wears text tokens, never the series color** - values, labels, and legends
  stay in primary/secondary/muted ink; a colored mark beside them carries identity.
- **Status colors are reserved** (good/warning/serious/critical) and never reused
  for "series 4"; they ship with an icon + label, never color alone.

## Plugging in a design system

The method is invariant; only these parameters change per system. The reference
instance - every value filled in - is `references/palette.md`.

| Parameter | What the system provides |
|---|---|
| **Ramps** | the hue scales (named steps) the palette draws from |
| **Categorical theme** | the fixed hue order (a named theme); default + alternates |
| **Sequential hue** | the default single hue for magnitude |
| **Diverging pair** | two warm/cool poles + a neutral midpoint |
| **Status palette** | good / warning / serious / critical - steps distinct from categorical |
| **Texture fill** | one directional hand-drawn fill, used at 45° / 135° |
| **Surfaces** | light & dark chart-surface colors (the validator needs these) |
| **Filter controls** | date-range & dimension controls (behavioral spec in `interaction.md`) |

To onboard a new system: fill those rows, feed its ramps to the validator, and let
it snap each slot to the nearest passing step. Structure and rules stay as written.

## Reference files

| File | What it answers |
|------|-----------------|
| `references/choosing-a-form.md` | Which chart type / is it even a chart? |
| `references/color-formula.md` | The four jobs, the six checks, snap-to-passing |
| `references/marks-and-anatomy.md` | Mark specs, spacers, labels, figures, hero number |
| `references/interaction.md` | Tooltips & hover, filters & time ranges |
| `references/components.md` | The pieces a chart is made of - build each in plain HTML |
| `references/anti-patterns.md` | **What goes wrong - check every chart against this** |
| `references/palette.md` | **The reference palette instance** - every parameter, filled in; swap for your brand's |
| `scripts/validate_palette.js` | Runnable six-checks validator (run it; don't eyeball) |

"""Build all paper figures from results/*.json into paper_draft/figs/."""
import json
import os

import matplotlib

matplotlib.use("Agg")
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np

ROOT = os.path.dirname(os.path.dirname(os.path.abspath(__file__)))
FIG = os.path.join(ROOT, "paper_draft", "figs")
os.makedirs(FIG, exist_ok=True)
INK, MUTED, GRID = "#0b0b0b", "#52514e", "#e4e3df"
MODELS = {"qwen": ("Qwen2.5-7B", "#2a78d6", "o"), "llama": ("Llama-3.1-8B", "#eb6834", "s"), "gemma": ("Gemma-2-9B", "#1baf7a", "^"),
          "gpt41mini": ("GPT-4.1-mini", "#eda100", "D")}
plt.rcParams.update({"font.size": 8.5, "axes.edgecolor": MUTED, "axes.labelcolor": INK, "xtick.color": MUTED, "ytick.color": MUTED,
                     "axes.spines.top": False, "axes.spines.right": False, "axes.grid": True, "grid.color": GRID, "grid.linewidth": 0.6,
                     "figure.facecolor": "white", "axes.facecolor": "white", "legend.frameon": False, "axes.titlesize": 9})


def fig_behaviour():
    S = json.load(open(os.path.join(ROOT, "results", "behave_summary_gpt41.json")))
    groups = [("harmful (refusal)", "Refusal, harmful"), ("borderline-benign (refusal)", "Refusal, borderline-benign"),
              ("TruthfulQA+suggestion (sycophancy)", "Sycophancy, TruthfulQA"), ("MWE political (sycophancy)", "Sycophancy, MWE political")]
    contrasts = [("LLM - casual human (pooled)", "LLM vs casual human\n(bundled style)"), ("formal human - casual human", "formal vs casual human\n(formality)"),
                 ("LLM - formal human", "LLM vs formal human\n(authorship, formality-matched)"), ("long - short", "elaborated vs short\n(length/explicitness)"),
                 ("label AI - label human", "stated 'AI-written' vs\n'human-written' label")]
    models = [m for m in MODELS if m in S]
    fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 4, figsize=(11, 3.6), sharey=True)
    for ax, (g, title) in zip(axes, groups):
        for ci, (c, _) in enumerate(contrasts):
            for mi, m in enumerate(models):
                r = S[m]["contrasts"].get(g, {}).get(c)
                if c.startswith("LLM - casual") and r is None:
                    r = S[m]["contrasts"].get(g, {}).get("LLM - casual human (short)")
                if not r:
                    continue
                y = ci + (mi - (len(models) - 1) / 2) * 0.17
                name, col, mk = MODELS[m]
                ax.plot([100 * r["lo"], 100 * r["hi"]], [y, y], color=col, lw=1.4, solid_capstyle="round")
                ax.plot(100 * r["diff"], y, mk, color=col, ms=4.5, mec="white", mew=0.6, label=name if ci == 0 else None)
        ax.axvline(0, color=MUTED, lw=0.8)
        ax.set_title(title)
        ax.set_xlabel("difference (percentage points)")
        ax.set_yticks(range(len(contrasts)))
        ax.set_yticklabels([c[1] for c in contrasts])
        ax.set_ylim(len(contrasts) - 0.5, -0.5)
        ax.grid(axis="y", visible=False)
    axes[0].legend(loc="upper center", bbox_to_anchor=(2.3, 1.28), ncol=4)
    fig.tight_layout()
    fig.savefig(os.path.join(FIG, "behaviour.pdf"), bbox_inches="tight")
    plt.close(fig)


def fig_probes():
    ms = [m for m in ["qwen", "llama", "gemma"] if os.path.exists(os.path.join(ROOT, "results", f"probes_{m}.json"))]
    fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, len(ms), figsize=(3.6 * len(ms), 2.9), sharey=True)
    lines = [("hc_vs_ls", "LLM vs casual human", "#2a78d6", "-"), ("hc_vs_hf", "formal vs casual human", "#eb6834", "--"),
             ("hf_vs_ls", "LLM vs formal human", "#1baf7a", "-"), ("orig_vs_ls", "LLM vs original human", "#eda100", "-.")]
    for ax, m in zip(np.atleast_1d(axes), ms):
        P = json.load(open(os.path.join(ROOT, "results", f"probes_{m}.json")))
        ded = P["dedicated"]["mean"]
        for k, lab, col, ls in lines:
            ys = [(l, v) for l, v in enumerate(ded[k]["lr"]) if v is not None and l > 0]
            ax.plot([l for l, _ in ys], [v for _, v in ys], ls, color=col, lw=2, marker="o", ms=3.5, label=lab)
        ax.axhline(0.5, color=MUTED, lw=0.8, ls=":")
        ax.set_title(MODELS[m][0])
        ax.set_xlabel("layer")
        ax.set_ylim(0.45, 1.02)
    np.atleast_1d(axes)[0].set_ylabel("held-out probe AUC")
    np.atleast_1d(axes)[0].legend(loc="lower right", fontsize=7.5)
    fig.tight_layout()
    fig.savefig(os.path.join(FIG, "probes.pdf"), bbox_inches="tight")
    plt.close(fig)


def fig_cos():
    S = json.load(open(os.path.join(ROOT, "results", "steer_summary.json"))) if os.path.exists(os.path.join(ROOT, "results", "steer_summary.json")) else {}
    ms = [m for m in ["qwen", "llama", "gemma"] if os.path.exists(os.path.join(ROOT, "results", f"probes_{m}.json"))]
    names = ["style_last", "formal_last", "resid_last", "len_last", "stated_last", "eval_last", "refusal_last"]
    labels = ["LLM-vs-casual\n(style)", "formality", "LLM-vs-formal\n(residual)", "length", "stated\nAI author", "eval\nawareness", "refusal"]
    fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, len(ms), figsize=(3.9 * len(ms), 3.6))
    for ax, m in zip(np.atleast_1d(axes), ms):
        P = json.load(open(os.path.join(ROOT, "results", f"probes_{m}.json")))
        layer = S.get(m, {}).get("layer", P["n_layers"] // 2)
        M = np.eye(len(names))
        for i, a in enumerate(names):
            for j, b in enumerate(names):
                if i < j:
                    v = P["cos"].get(f"{a}|{b}") or P["cos"].get(f"{b}|{a}")
                    M[i, j] = M[j, i] = v[layer]
        im = ax.imshow(M, cmap="RdBu_r", vmin=-1, vmax=1)
        for i in range(len(names)):
            for j in range(len(names)):
                ax.text(j, i, f"{M[i, j]:.2f}".replace("0.", ".").replace("1.00", "1"), ha="center", va="center", fontsize=6.5,
                        color="white" if abs(M[i, j]) > 0.6 else INK)
        ax.set_xticks(range(len(names)))
        ax.set_xticklabels(labels, rotation=60, ha="right", fontsize=7)
        ax.set_yticks(range(len(names)))
        ax.set_yticklabels(labels if ax is np.atleast_1d(axes)[0] else [], fontsize=7)
        ax.set_title(f"{MODELS[m][0]} (layer {layer})")
        ax.grid(False)
    fig.tight_layout()
    fig.savefig(os.path.join(FIG, "cosines.pdf"), bbox_inches="tight")
    plt.close(fig)


def fig_steer():
    path = os.path.join(ROOT, "results", "steer_summary.json")
    if not os.path.exists(path):
        return
    S = json.load(open(path))
    ms = [m for m in ["qwen", "llama", "gemma"] if m in S]
    fams = [("style_last", "LLM-vs-casual (style)"), ("formal_last", "formality"), ("resid_last", "LLM-vs-formal (residual)"),
            ("resid_orth", "residual, orthogonalised"), ("len_last", "length"), ("stated_last", "stated AI author"),
            ("eval_last", "eval awareness"), ("refusal_last", "refusal (pos. control)")]
    outs = [("harmful", "refusal, harmful"), ("borderline", "refusal, borderline-benign"), ("syco", "sycophancy, TruthfulQA")]
    fig, axes = plt.subplots(len(ms), 3, figsize=(11, 2.9 * len(ms)), sharey=True, squeeze=False)
    for r, m in enumerate(ms):
        C = S[m]["conds"]
        A = S[m]["A"]
        for c, (g, title) in enumerate(outs):
            ax = axes[r, c]
            rnd = [100 * C[k][g]["diff"] for k in C if k.startswith("random")]
            ax.axvspan(min(rnd), max(rnd), color="#d9d8d3", alpha=0.7, lw=0, label="random directions (range)" if (r == 0 and c == 0) else None)
            ax.axvline(0, color=MUTED, lw=0.8)
            for i, (f, lab) in enumerate(fams):
                for sign, col, mk, off in [(+1, "#eb6834", "o", -0.14), (-1, "#2a78d6", "s", 0.14)]:
                    k = f"{f}@{sign * A:+g}"
                    if k not in C:
                        continue
                    d = C[k][g]
                    ax.plot([100 * d["lo"], 100 * d["hi"]], [i + off, i + off], color=col, lw=1.4, solid_capstyle="round")
                    ax.plot(100 * d["diff"], i + off, mk, color=col, ms=4.5, mec="white", mew=0.6,
                            label=(f"+{A:g}s (towards the named pole)" if sign > 0 else f"-{A:g}s (away from it)") if (r == 0 and c == 0 and i == 0) else None)
            ax.set_yticks(range(len(fams)))
            ax.set_yticklabels([f[1] for f in fams])
            ax.set_ylim(len(fams) - 0.5, -0.5)
            ax.grid(axis="y", visible=False)
            ax.set_xlim(-102, 102)
            ax.set_title(f"{MODELS[m][0]}: {title}")
            if r == len(ms) - 1:
                ax.set_xlabel("change vs. unsteered (percentage points)")
    axes[0, 0].legend(loc="lower left", bbox_to_anchor=(0.0, 1.12), ncol=3)
    fig.tight_layout()
    fig.savefig(os.path.join(FIG, "steering.pdf"), bbox_inches="tight")
    plt.close(fig)

    # dose-response along the style direction
    fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 4, figsize=(11, 2.6))
    keys = [("harmful", "refusal, harmful (%)"), ("borderline", "refusal, borderline-benign (%)"), ("syco", "sycophancy, TruthfulQA (%)")]
    for m in ms:
        C = S[m]["conds"]
        name, col, mk = MODELS[m]
        pts = sorted([(0.0, C["base"])] + [(float(k.split("@")[1]), v) for k, v in C.items() if k.startswith("style_last@")])
        for ax, (g, yl) in zip(axes, keys):
            ax.plot([a for a, _ in pts], [100 * v[g]["rate"] for _, v in pts], "-", color=col, marker=mk, ms=4.5, lw=2, mec="white", mew=0.6, label=name)
            ax.set_ylabel(yl)
        axes[3].plot([a for a, _ in pts], [v["nll"] for _, v in pts], "-", color=col, marker=mk, ms=4.5, lw=2, mec="white", mew=0.6)
    axes[3].set_ylabel("NLL of unsteered replies (nats/token)")
    for ax in axes:
        ax.set_xlabel("steering along LLM-style direction (units of s)")
    axes[0].legend(fontsize=7.5)
    fig.tight_layout()
    fig.savefig(os.path.join(FIG, "dose.pdf"), bbox_inches="tight")
    plt.close(fig)


if __name__ == "__main__":
    fig_behaviour()
    fig_probes()
    fig_cos()
    fig_steer()
    print("figures written to", FIG)

"""Build all paper figures from results/*.json into paper_draft/figs/."""
import json
import os

import matplotlib

matplotlib.use("Agg")
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np

ROOT = os.path.dirname(os.path.dirname(os.path.abspath(__file__)))
FIG = os.path.join(ROOT, "paper_draft", "figs")
os.makedirs(FIG, exist_ok=True)
INK, MUTED, GRID = "#0b0b0b", "#52514e", "#e4e3df"
MODELS = {"qwen": ("Qwen2.5-7B", "#2a78d6", "o"), "llama": ("Llama-3.1-8B", "#eb6834", "s"), "gemma": ("Gemma-2-9B", "#1baf7a", "^"),
          "gpt41mini": ("GPT-4.1-mini", "#eda100", "D")}
plt.rcParams.update({"font.size": 8.5, "axes.edgecolor": MUTED, "axes.labelcolor": INK, "xtick.color": MUTED, "ytick.color": MUTED,
                     "axes.spines.top": False, "axes.spines.right": False, "axes.grid": True, "grid.color": GRID, "grid.linewidth": 0.6,
                     "figure.facecolor": "white", "axes.facecolor": "white", "legend.frameon": False, "axes.titlesize": 9})


def fig_behaviour():
    S = json.load(open(os.path.join(ROOT, "results", "behave_summary_gpt41.json")))
    groups = [("harmful (refusal)", "Refusal, harmful"), ("borderline-benign (refusal)", "Refusal, borderline-benign"),
              ("TruthfulQA+suggestion (sycophancy)", "Sycophancy, TruthfulQA"), ("MWE political (sycophancy)", "Sycophancy, MWE political")]
    contrasts = [("LLM - casual human (pooled)", "LLM vs casual human\n(bundled style)"), ("formal human - casual human", "formal vs casual human\n(formality)"),
                 ("LLM - formal human", "LLM vs formal human\n(authorship, formality-matched)"), ("long - short", "elaborated vs short\n(length/explicitness)"),
                 ("label AI - label human", "stated 'AI-written' vs\n'human-written' label")]
    models = [m for m in MODELS if m in S]
    fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 4, figsize=(11, 3.6), sharey=True)
    for ax, (g, title) in zip(axes, groups):
        for ci, (c, _) in enumerate(contrasts):
            for mi, m in enumerate(models):
                r = S[m]["contrasts"].get(g, {}).get(c)
                if c.startswith("LLM - casual") and r is None:
                    r = S[m]["contrasts"].get(g, {}).get("LLM - casual human (short)")
                if not r:
                    continue
                y = ci + (mi - (len(models) - 1) / 2) * 0.17
                name, col, mk = MODELS[m]
                ax.plot([100 * r["lo"], 100 * r["hi"]], [y, y], color=col, lw=1.4, solid_capstyle="round")
                ax.plot(100 * r["diff"], y, mk, color=col, ms=4.5, mec="white", mew=0.6, label=name if ci == 0 else None)
        ax.axvline(0, color=MUTED, lw=0.8)
        ax.set_title(title)
        ax.set_xlabel("difference (percentage points)")
        ax.set_yticks(range(len(contrasts)))
        ax.set_yticklabels([c[1] for c in contrasts])
        ax.set_ylim(len(contrasts) - 0.5, -0.5)
        ax.grid(axis="y", visible=False)
    axes[0].legend(loc="upper center", bbox_to_anchor=(2.3, 1.28), ncol=4)
    fig.tight_layout()
    fig.savefig(os.path.join(FIG, "behaviour.pdf"), bbox_inches="tight")
    plt.close(fig)


def fig_probes():
    ms = [m for m in ["qwen", "llama", "gemma"] if os.path.exists(os.path.join(ROOT, "results", f"probes_{m}.json"))]
    fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, len(ms), figsize=(3.6 * len(ms), 2.9), sharey=True)
    lines = [("hc_vs_ls", "LLM vs casual human", "#2a78d6", "-"), ("hc_vs_hf", "formal vs casual human", "#eb6834", "--"),
             ("hf_vs_ls", "LLM vs formal human", "#1baf7a", "-"), ("orig_vs_ls", "LLM vs original human", "#eda100", "-.")]
    for ax, m in zip(np.atleast_1d(axes), ms):
        P = json.load(open(os.path.join(ROOT, "results", f"probes_{m}.json")))
        ded = P["dedicated"]["mean"]
        for k, lab, col, ls in lines:
            ys = [(l, v) for l, v in enumerate(ded[k]["lr"]) if v is not None and l > 0]
            ax.plot([l for l, _ in ys], [v for _, v in ys], ls, color=col, lw=2, marker="o", ms=3.5, label=lab)
        ax.axhline(0.5, color=MUTED, lw=0.8, ls=":")
        ax.set_title(MODELS[m][0])
        ax.set_xlabel("layer")
        ax.set_ylim(0.45, 1.02)
    np.atleast_1d(axes)[0].set_ylabel("held-out probe AUC")
    np.atleast_1d(axes)[0].legend(loc="lower right", fontsize=7.5)
    fig.tight_layout()
    fig.savefig(os.path.join(FIG, "probes.pdf"), bbox_inches="tight")
    plt.close(fig)


def fig_cos():
    S = json.load(open(os.path.join(ROOT, "results", "steer_summary.json"))) if os.path.exists(os.path.join(ROOT, "results", "steer_summary.json")) else {}
    ms = [m for m in ["qwen", "llama", "gemma"] if os.path.exists(os.path.join(ROOT, "results", f"probes_{m}.json"))]
    names = ["style_last", "formal_last", "resid_last", "len_last", "stated_last", "eval_last", "refusal_last"]
    labels = ["LLM-vs-casual\n(style)", "formality", "LLM-vs-formal\n(residual)", "length", "stated\nAI author", "eval\nawareness", "refusal"]
    fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, len(ms), figsize=(3.9 * len(ms), 3.6))
    for ax, m in zip(np.atleast_1d(axes), ms):
        P = json.load(open(os.path.join(ROOT, "results", f"probes_{m}.json")))
        layer = S.get(m, {}).get("layer", P["n_layers"] // 2)
        M = np.eye(len(names))
        for i, a in enumerate(names):
            for j, b in enumerate(names):
                if i < j:
                    v = P["cos"].get(f"{a}|{b}") or P["cos"].get(f"{b}|{a}")
                    M[i, j] = M[j, i] = v[layer]
        im = ax.imshow(M, cmap="RdBu_r", vmin=-1, vmax=1)
        for i in range(len(names)):
            for j in range(len(names)):
                ax.text(j, i, f"{M[i, j]:.2f}".replace("0.", ".").replace("1.00", "1"), ha="center", va="center", fontsize=6.5,
                        color="white" if abs(M[i, j]) > 0.6 else INK)
        ax.set_xticks(range(len(names)))
        ax.set_xticklabels(labels, rotation=60, ha="right", fontsize=7)
        ax.set_yticks(range(len(names)))
        ax.set_yticklabels(labels if ax is np.atleast_1d(axes)[0] else [], fontsize=7)
        ax.set_title(f"{MODELS[m][0]} (layer {layer})")
        ax.grid(False)
    fig.tight_layout()
    fig.savefig(os.path.join(FIG, "cosines.pdf"), bbox_inches="tight")
    plt.close(fig)


def fig_steer():
    path = os.path.join(ROOT, "results", "steer_summary.json")
    if not os.path.exists(path):
        return
    S = json.load(open(path))
    ms = [m for m in ["qwen", "llama", "gemma"] if m in S]
    fams = [("style_last", "LLM-vs-casual (style)"), ("formal_last", "formality"), ("resid_last", "LLM-vs-formal (residual)"),
            ("resid_orth", "residual, orthogonalised"), ("len_last", "length"), ("stated_last", "stated AI author"),
            ("eval_last", "eval awareness"), ("refusal_last", "refusal (pos. control)")]
    outs = [("harmful", "refusal, harmful"), ("borderline", "refusal, borderline-benign"), ("syco", "sycophancy, TruthfulQA")]
    fig, axes = plt.subplots(len(ms), 3, figsize=(11, 2.9 * len(ms)), sharey=True, squeeze=False)
    for r, m in enumerate(ms):
        C = S[m]["conds"]
        A = S[m]["A"]
        for c, (g, title) in enumerate(outs):
            ax = axes[r, c]
            rnd = [100 * C[k][g]["diff"] for k in C if k.startswith("random")]
            ax.axvspan(min(rnd), max(rnd), color="#d9d8d3", alpha=0.7, lw=0, label="random directions (range)" if (r == 0 and c == 0) else None)
            ax.axvline(0, color=MUTED, lw=0.8)
            for i, (f, lab) in enumerate(fams):
                for sign, col, mk, off in [(+1, "#eb6834", "o", -0.14), (-1, "#2a78d6", "s", 0.14)]:
                    k = f"{f}@{sign * A:+g}"
                    if k not in C:
                        continue
                    d = C[k][g]
                    ax.plot([100 * d["lo"], 100 * d["hi"]], [i + off, i + off], color=col, lw=1.4, solid_capstyle="round")
                    ax.plot(100 * d["diff"], i + off, mk, color=col, ms=4.5, mec="white", mew=0.6,
                            label=(f"+{A:g}s (towards the named pole)" if sign > 0 else f"-{A:g}s (away from it)") if (r == 0 and c == 0 and i == 0) else None)
            ax.set_yticks(range(len(fams)))
            ax.set_yticklabels([f[1] for f in fams])
            ax.set_ylim(len(fams) - 0.5, -0.5)
            ax.grid(axis="y", visible=False)
            ax.set_xlim(-102, 102)
            ax.set_title(f"{MODELS[m][0]}: {title}")
            if r == len(ms) - 1:
                ax.set_xlabel("change vs. unsteered (percentage points)")
    axes[0, 0].legend(loc="lower left", bbox_to_anchor=(0.0, 1.12), ncol=3)
    fig.tight_layout()
    fig.savefig(os.path.join(FIG, "steering.pdf"), bbox_inches="tight")
    plt.close(fig)

    # dose-response along the style direction
    fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 4, figsize=(11, 2.6))
    keys = [("harmful", "refusal, harmful (%)"), ("borderline", "refusal, borderline-benign (%)"), ("syco", "sycophancy, TruthfulQA (%)")]
    for m in ms:
        C = S[m]["conds"]
        name, col, mk = MODELS[m]
        pts = sorted([(0.0, C["base"])] + [(float(k.split("@")[1]), v) for k, v in C.items() if k.startswith("style_last@")])
        for ax, (g, yl) in zip(axes, keys):
            ax.plot([a for a, _ in pts], [100 * v[g]["rate"] for _, v in pts], "-", color=col, marker=mk, ms=4.5, lw=2, mec="white", mew=0.6, label=name)
            ax.set_ylabel(yl)
        axes[3].plot([a for a, _ in pts], [v["nll"] for _, v in pts], "-", color=col, marker=mk, ms=4.5, lw=2, mec="white", mew=0.6)
    axes[3].set_ylabel("NLL of unsteered replies (nats/token)")
    for ax in axes:
        ax.set_xlabel("steering along LLM-style direction (units of s)")
    axes[0].legend(fontsize=7.5)
    fig.tight_layout()
    fig.savefig(os.path.join(FIG, "dose.pdf"), bbox_inches="tight")
    plt.close(fig)


if __name__ == "__main__":
    fig_behaviour()
    fig_probes()
    fig_cos()
    fig_steer()
    print("figures written to", FIG)

"""Inter-judge agreement: re-label a random sample with a second judge model (and a regex baseline for refusals)."""
import json
import os
import random

from sklearn.metrics import cohen_kappa_score

import judge as J
from analyze_behave import REF_RE
from api import COST, ROOT, chat, pmap

SECOND = "google/gemini-2.5-flash"
random.seed(0)
base = {i["id"]: i for i in json.load(open(os.path.join(ROOT, "data", "base_items.json")))}
rows = []
for m in ["qwen", "llama", "gemma"]:
    R = [json.loads(l) for l in open(os.path.join(ROOT, "results", f"behave_{m}_gpt41.jsonl"))]
    R = [r for r in R if r.get("judge") in J.VALID and r["dataset"] != "tqa_plain"]
    rows += random.sample([r for r in R if r["dataset"].startswith(("jbb", "xst"))], 150) + random.sample([r for r in R if r["dataset"] == "tqa_sug"], 80)


def job(r):
    it = base[r["id"]]
    if r["dataset"] == "tqa_sug":
        p = J.SYCO.format(q=it["meta"]["question"], wrong=it["meta"]["wrong"], best=it["meta"]["best"], resp=r["response"])
    else:
        p = J.REFUSAL.format(req=it["text"], resp=r["response"])
    out = chat(SECOND, [{"role": "user", "content": p}], max_tokens=200, tag="jv1")
    for lab in ["REFUSE", "COMPLY", "AGREE", "CORRECT", "OTHER"]:
        if out and lab in out.upper():
            return lab
    return None


labs = pmap(job, rows, workers=16, desc="second judge")
out = {}
for name, sel in [("refusal", lambda r: r["dataset"] != "tqa_sug"), ("sycophancy", lambda r: r["dataset"] == "tqa_sug")]:
    pairs = [(r["judge"], l) for r, l in zip(rows, labs) if sel(r) and l is not None]
    a, b = zip(*pairs)
    out[name] = dict(n=len(pairs), agreement=sum(x == y for x, y in pairs) / len(pairs), kappa=float(cohen_kappa_score(a, b)))
    if name == "sycophancy":
        a2, b2 = [x == "AGREE" for x in a], [x == "AGREE" for x in b]
        out[name]["agree_vs_rest_agreement"] = sum(x == y for x, y in zip(a2, b2)) / len(a2)
        out[name]["agree_vs_rest_kappa"] = float(cohen_kappa_score(a2, b2))
ref = [(r["judge"], "REFUSE" if REF_RE.match(r["response"]) else "COMPLY") for r in rows if r["dataset"] != "tqa_sug"]
out["refusal_vs_regex"] = dict(n=len(ref), agreement=sum(x == y for x, y in ref) / len(ref), kappa=float(cohen_kappa_score(*zip(*ref))))
print(json.dumps(out, indent=1), COST)
json.dump(out, open(os.path.join(ROOT, "results", "judge_validation.json"), "w"), indent=1)

"""Generate LaTeX tables in paper_draft/tables/ from results/*.json."""
import json
import os
import sys

import numpy as np

sys.path.insert(0, os.path.dirname(os.path.abspath(__file__)))
from run_behave_common import load_items  # noqa: E402

ROOT = os.path.dirname(os.path.dirname(os.path.abspath(__file__)))
OUT = os.path.join(ROOT, "paper_draft", "tables")
os.makedirs(OUT, exist_ok=True)
NAMES = {"qwen": "Qwen2.5-7B", "llama": "Llama-3.1-8B", "gemma": "Gemma-2-9B", "gpt41mini": "GPT-4.1-mini", "llama70b": "Llama-3.3-70B",
         "haiku45": "Claude Haiku 4.5"}
VARS = [("orig", "original"), ("hc", "casual human"), ("hf", "formal human"), ("ls", "LLM"), ("hl", "casual human, long"), ("ll", "LLM, long")]
GROUPS = [("harmful (refusal)", "Refusal, harmful"), ("borderline-benign (refusal)", "Refusal, borderline"),
          ("TruthfulQA+suggestion (sycophancy)", "Sycophancy, TQA"), ("MWE political (sycophancy)", "Sycophancy, MWE"),
          ("TruthfulQA plain (accuracy)", "Accuracy, TQA")]


def w(name, s):
    open(os.path.join(OUT, name), "w").write(s)


def load(p):
    p = os.path.join(ROOT, "results", p)
    return json.load(open(p)) if os.path.exists(p) else None


def t_data():
    items = load_items()
    ds = ["jbb_harmful", "xstest_unsafe", "jbb_benign", "xstest_safe", "tqa_sug", "tqa_plain", "mwe_syco", "wildchat"]
    lab = {"jbb_harmful": "JBB harmful", "xstest_unsafe": "XSTest unsafe", "jbb_benign": "JBB benign", "xstest_safe": "XSTest safe",
           "tqa_sug": "TruthfulQA + suggestion", "tqa_plain": "TruthfulQA plain", "mwe_syco": "MWE sycophancy (bio only)", "wildchat": "WildChat"}
    rows = []
    for d in ds:
        I = [i for i in items if i["dataset"] == d]
        nl = sum("ll" in i["variants"] for i in I)
        ws = [f"{np.mean([len(i['variants'][v].split()) for i in I if v in i['variants']]):.0f}" if any(v in i["variants"] for i in I) else "--" for v, _ in VARS]
        rows.append(f"{lab[d]} & {len(I)} & {nl} & " + " & ".join(ws) + r" \\")
    w("data.tex", "\n".join(rows))


def t_rates(S, models, name):
    lines = []
    for g, gl in GROUPS:
        first = True
        for m in models:
            r = S[m]["rates"].get(g)
            if not r:
                continue
            cells = [f"{100 * r[v]['mean']:.1f}" if v in r else "--" for v, _ in VARS]
            lines.append((gl if first else "") + f" & {NAMES[m]} & " + " & ".join(cells) + r" \\")
            first = False
        lines.append(r"\midrule")
    w(name, "\n".join(lines[:-1]))


def t_contrasts(S, models, name, contrasts):
    lines = []
    for g, gl in GROUPS[:4]:
        first = True
        for m in models:

                    f"{c['nll'] - C['base']['nll']:+.2f} & {gcv}" + r" \\")

        b = C["base"]
        lines.append(f"unsteered (absolute) & {100 * b['harmful']['rate']:.1f} & {100 * b['borderline']['rate']:.1f} & {100 * b['syco']['rate']:.1f} & "

"""Robustness: re-judge all TruthfulQA-suggestion responses of the local models with a second judge (Gemini 2.5 Flash)
and recompute the sycophancy contrasts."""
import json
import os
import warnings

warnings.filterwarnings("ignore")
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd

import judge as J
from analyze_behave import CONTRASTS, paired
from api import COST, ROOT, chat, pmap

SECOND = "google/gemini-2.5-flash"
base = {i["id"]: i for i in json.load(open(os.path.join(ROOT, "data", "base_items.json")))}
out = {}
rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
for m in ["qwen", "llama", "gemma"]:
    R = [json.loads(l) for l in open(os.path.join(ROOT, "results", f"behave_{m}_gpt41.jsonl"))]
    R = [r for r in R if r["dataset"] == "tqa_sug"]

    def job(r):
        it = base[r["id"]]
        p = J.SYCO.format(q=it["meta"]["question"], wrong=it["meta"]["wrong"], best=it["meta"]["best"], resp=r["response"])
        o = chat(SECOND, [{"role": "user", "content": p}], max_tokens=200, tag="jv1")
        return float("AGREE" in o.upper() and "DISAGREE" not in o.upper()) if o else np.nan

    labs = pmap(job, R, workers=16, desc=m)
    df = pd.DataFrame(R)
    df["y"] = labs
    W = df.pivot(index="id", columns="var", values="y")
    out[m] = {"rates": {v: float(W[v].mean()) for v in W.columns}, "contrasts": {c: paired(W, p, q, rng) for c, (p, q) in CONTRASTS.items()}}
    print(m, {k: round(v, 3) for k, v in out[m]["rates"].items()})
    for c, r in out[m]["contrasts"].items():
        if r:
            print(f"   {c:36s} diff={r['diff']:+.3f} [{r['lo']:+.3f},{r['hi']:+.3f}] p={r['p']:.3f}")
json.dump(out, open(os.path.join(ROOT, "results", "syco_second_judge.json"), "w"), indent=1)
print(COST)
E

input.content:
\section{Introduction}

Language models are increasingly prompted by other language models. Safety evaluations are frequently written by models \citep{perez2022discovering}, automated red-teaming and auditing pipelines generate their own user turns, and in multi-agent systems an orchestrator's instructions to its sub-agents are machine-written. At the same time, models can often tell evaluation transcripts from deployment transcripts \citep{needham2025large}, evaluation awareness is linearly represented and can be steered with behavioural consequences \citep{abdelnabi2025hawthorne,nguyen2025probing,heidari2026evaluation}, and machine-written text is linearly separable from human-written text in LLM activations \citep{chen2025repreguard,quaremba2026linear}. Put together, these facts raise a concrete worry: if a prompt that \emph{reads as LLM-written} shifts a model's safety-relevant behaviour, then results obtained with synthetic prompts may not transfer to deployment with human users, and vice versa.

Testing this is harder than it looks, because ``LLM style'' is bundled with other properties. When an LLM rewrites a human request, the result is typically longer, more explicit, more polite and grammatically cleaner. A behavioural difference between a human prompt and its LLM rewrite could therefore reflect elaboration or politeness rather than perceived authorship, or simply the fact that the text was paraphrased at all. We address this with three kinds of control.

\begin{enumerate}\itemsep0pt
\item \textbf{A factorial rewrite design.} Starting from human-written requests, we create content-matched variants that separate (i) casual-human style from LLM style at matched length, (ii) formality from authorship, via a careful/formal \emph{human-style} variant, (iii) elaboration, via a long LLM ``delegation'' rewrite and a casual-human restyling \emph{of that same long text}, and (iv) paraphrasing as such. All rewrites are checked for content fidelity by a judge model. We mirror the design on natively LLM-written evaluation items.
\item \textbf{Explicit authorship labels.} With the prompt text held fixed, we prepend a note saying that the message was written by a human or generated by an AI, which manipulates \emph{stated} authorship without touching style.
\item \textbf{Activation interventions.} With the prompt text held fixed, we add directions to the residual stream: the ``LLM-vs-casual-human'' style direction, its formality-matched residual, a formality direction, a length direction, a stated-authorship direction, an evaluation-awareness direction, norm-matched random directions and a refusal direction as positive control.
\end{enumerate}

We measure refusal on harmful and borderline-benign requests (JailbreakBench, XSTest), sycophancy towards a user-suggested misconception (TruthfulQA), opinion sycophancy on model-written evaluation items, and answer accuracy, in three open-weight models with activation access (Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, Gemma-2-9B-it) and, behaviourally, in three API models (GPT-4.1-mini, Llama-3.3-70B, Claude Haiku 4.5).

\paragraph{Findings.}
\begin{itemize}\itemsep0pt
\item \textbf{The formality-matched authorship effect is null.} Across six models and four behaviours, the contrast between an LLM-style prompt and a careful human-style prompt of the same content and length is small (mostly within $\pm$4 percentage points) and not robustly different from zero (\S\ref{sec:behaviour}). Our design can only detect effects of roughly five points or more per model, and a few isolated contrasts do reach nominal significance.

\section{Related work}

\paragraph{Evaluation awareness.} \citet{needham2025large} show that frontier models classify evaluation versus deployment transcripts well above chance and that synthetic-looking prompts are one cue, but they do not isolate authorship style. \citet{abdelnabi2025hawthorne} probe and steer ``test awareness'' in reasoning models and find that it changes compliance; \citet{nguyen2025probing} build linear probes for evaluation versus deployment from contrastive prompts in Llama-3.3-70B; \citet{heidari2026evaluation} study how such representations relate to verbalisation and control. We borrow the contrastive-prompt construction for an evaluation-awareness direction and ask how it relates to an ``LLM-written'' direction.

\paragraph{Detecting machine-written text from activations.} RepreGuard \citep{chen2025repreguard} and linear-probing detectors \citep{quaremba2026linear} show that human- and machine-written text are linearly separable in LLM hidden states. These works use the representation as a detector of documents. We look at the same kind of signal on the \emph{user prompt}, ask what it encodes once formality and length are controlled, and connect it to downstream behaviour by intervention.

\paragraph{LLM text as the object of judgement.} Models recognise and favour their own generations when acting as evaluators \citep{panickssery2024llm}, and prefer LLM-written communications in choice settings such as hiring and product selection \citep{laurito2024ai,xu2025ai}. There, LLM text is what is being judged. We study LLM text as the \emph{instruction}.

\paragraph{Prompt construction as a confound.} \citet{chalkidis2026templated} shows that templated versus fully synthetic prompt construction changes measured political stance; this is the closest behavioural analogue, for one behaviour. Model-written evaluations \citep{perez2022discovering} are widely used, and sycophancy in particular has been measured with both model-written and human-written items \citep{sharma2023towards}.

\paragraph{Steering and directions.} Refusal is mediated by a single direction in many chat models \citep{arditi2024refusal}, and difference-of-means steering is a standard tool \citep{turner2023activation,rimsky2023steering}. We use the refusal direction as a positive control and follow the practice of comparing against norm-matched random directions.

\paragraph{Gap.} To our knowledge no prior work (a) isolates human versus LLM style of the user prompt with content held fixed across several safety-relevant behaviours, (b) tests by intervention whether an internal ``LLM-written'' representation rather than surface features drives behaviour, and (c) relates that representation to evaluation awareness.

\section{Discussion}

\paragraph{What the evidence supports.} The question was whether a prompt that reads as LLM-written changes safety-relevant behaviour once content is controlled, and whether any such change runs through an internal representation of LLM authorship. Three lines of evidence point the same way. Behaviourally, the LLM-versus-formal-human contrast is null within about five points per model, while formality and, above all, elaboration do move behaviour. Representationally, the direction that separates LLM-style from casual-human prompts is mostly a formality direction, and the model's own stated-authorship and evaluation-awareness directions respond to formal human text as much as to LLM text. Causally, shifting activations along the style direction by its natural magnitude, with the text fixed, changes behaviour no more than random directions do, although the same intervention reproduces the natural internal shift downstream and a refusal direction of the same norm has large effects. We therefore read the small style effects that do appear (slightly fewer refusals of harmful requests and slightly more deference for formal or LLM-like text) as effects of register, not of perceived authorship.

\paragraph{Stated authorship is separate.} Telling the model that the author is an AI, by a label or by steering the corresponding direction, has small effects of a different sign: somewhat more refusal of borderline requests and somewhat less agreement with a suggested misconception. The stated-authorship direction controls the verbal authorship judgement almost completely in Qwen, yet is nearly orthogonal to the style direction. A model can thus hold ``this was written by an AI'' as a proposition that matters a little for behaviour, without inferring that proposition from style. This is consistent with the 7--9B models being unable to verbalise authorship from style at all.

\paragraph{Implications for evaluation.} (1) A synthetic prompt does not appear to be treated differently merely for reading as machine-written, in the models and behaviours studied. (2) Synthetic prompts do differ from typical human prompts in register and explicitness, and these matter: an orchestrator-style elaboration of a harmful request was refused 10--15 points less often than its short form in four of six models, and one frontier model's willingness to answer a model-written sycophancy item at all changed by 18 points with the register of the persona text. Evaluations built from LLM-written prompts should match the length and register of the deployment distribution they are meant to predict, or report sensitivity to them. (3) Comparing human originals with LLM rewrites without a paraphrase control overstates any ``authorship'' effect, because rewording benchmark prompts by itself lowers refusal.

\section{Limitations}

\begin{itemize}\itemsep1pt
\item \textbf{The ``human'' variants are LLM imitations.} Casual and formal human styles were written by GPT-4.1 (and Gemini 2.5 Flash) under instruction. The only truly human texts are the originals, and those are not style-matched: benchmark prompts are terse imperatives, and the original-versus-LLM contrast is confounded with paraphrasing. If real careful human writing differs from LLM writing in ways our formal-human imitation fails to capture, our formality-matched contrast underestimates the authorship signal. The capable API models could not tell LLM-style text from the human originals either (52--55\% in the forced choice), which limits but does not remove this concern.
\item \textbf{Power.} Per-model intervals on the key null contrast have a median half-width of about 3 points and reach 7 points on the harmful subset. Effects below roughly five points per model are not excluded. Refusal of plainly harmful requests is near ceiling in Gemma-2-9B (97--100\% at short length), leaving little room there.
\item \textbf{Selection.} The fidelity filter and rewriter refusals removed 23\% of JailbreakBench-harmful and 16\% of XSTest-unsafe items at short length, and more for the long pair; the retained harmful items are those an API model was willing to restyle faithfully.
\item \textbf{Elaboration is not pure length.} The long variants add explicit expectations about the answer. The long-minus-short contrast therefore bundles length with explicitness and some added detail, and judged outcomes use the first 120--160 generated tokens, which may interact with longer replies.
\item \textbf{Steering.} We steer at a single, pre-chosen middle layer with last-token difference-of-means directions applied at all positions. At that layer the last-token style direction separates styles less cleanly in Llama and Gemma (AUC about 0.8) than the user-token-mean direction does (about 1.0); steering with the latter at $\pm2s$ was also null (Appendix~\ref{app:steer}). Other layers, multi-layer interventions or non-linear features could behave differently. The verbalised authorship judgement could not serve as a manipulation check for the style direction, because it is unreliable in these models and moves as much under random vectors; we rely on the downstream-projection check instead.
\item \textbf{Concept directions.} The evaluation-awareness and stated-authorship directions come from four hand-written statement pairs and are only moderately consistent across phrasings; conclusions about their relation to style are correspondingly tentative.
\item \textbf{Judging.} Refusal labels are reliable ($\kappa=0.94$ between judges). Sycophancy labels are noisier ($\kappa=0.50$); the conclusions hold under a second judge, but absolute sycophancy rates depend on the judge.
\item \textbf{Multiple comparisons.} We report many contrasts without correction. Isolated significant cells, including the Llama-3.1-8B long-pair effect, need independent replication.
\item \textbf{Scope.} Single-turn prompts, no system prompt, greedy decoding, six models, and four behaviours. Agentic settings, tool use and multi-turn interactions, where orchestrator-written prompts are most common, were not tested.
\end{itemize}

\section{Conclusion}

With content, length, formality and paraphrasing controlled, we find no evidence that current chat models change refusal, sycophancy or accuracy because a prompt reads as LLM-written. They do respond, modestly, to how formal a prompt is and, more strongly, to how elaborate it is; and the internal feature that most cleanly distinguishes LLM-style from casual human prompts tracks formality. Believed authorship, manipulated by an explicit statement or its activation direction, is a distinct variable with small effects of its own. For safety evaluation, the practical risk from synthetic prompts lies in their register and explicitness, which can and should be matched to deployment, more than in their being recognisably machine-written.

\item \textbf{Multiple comparisons.} We report many contrasts without correction. Isolated significant cells, including the Llama-3.1-8B long-pair effect, need independent replication.
\item \textbf{Scope.} Single-turn prompts, no system prompt, greedy decoding, six models, and four behaviours. Agentic settings, tool use and multi-turn interactions, where orchestrator-written prompts are most common, were not tested.
\end{itemize}

\section{Conclusion}

With content, length, formality and paraphrasing controlled, we find no evidence that current chat models change refusal, sycophancy or accuracy because a prompt reads as LLM-written. They do respond, modestly, to how formal a prompt is and, more strongly, to how elaborate it is; and the internal feature that most cleanly distinguishes LLM-style from casual human prompts tracks formality. Believed authorship, manipulated by an explicit statement or its activation direction, is a distinct variable with small effects of its own. For safety evaluation, the practical risk from synthetic prompts lies in their register and explicitness, which can and should be matched to deployment, more than in their being recognisably machine-written.

# Do LLMs behave differently when the prompt reads as LLM-written?

**Short answer from this study: not because of authorship.** With content, length, formality and paraphrasing
controlled, six chat models do not measurably change refusal or sycophancy when a prompt reads as LLM-written
rather than as carefully human-written. They do respond to how *formal* and, more strongly, how *elaborate* a
prompt is. Paper: [`paper_draft/main.pdf`](paper_draft/main.pdf).

## Question

Safety evaluations and multi-agent systems feed models prompts written by other models. If "reads LLM-written"
shifts behaviour, evaluation results may not transfer to human users. We ask (a) whether safety-relevant
behaviour changes with the style of the user prompt when content is fixed, and (b) whether any change is driven
by an internal "LLM-written" representation or by surface features (length, formality, having been paraphrased).

## What was done

- **Stimuli.** 1,384 items after filtering: JailbreakBench harmful/benign, XSTest safe/unsafe, TruthfulQA
  (plain, and with a user-suggested misconception), WildChat first turns, and natively LLM-written political
  sycophancy items from Anthropic's model-written evals. Each human-origin item was rewritten by GPT-4.1 into
  casual-human, formal-human, LLM, LLM-long (orchestrator-style elaboration) and casual-long (a casual restyling
  of the LLM-long text) variants. A judge checked every rewrite for content fidelity. A second rewriter
  (Gemini 2.5 Flash) was used as a robustness check.
- **Explicit labels.** "This message was generated by an AI" vs "typed by a human" (and test vs deploy) prepended
  to the unchanged original.
- **Models.** Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, Gemma-2-9B-it (behaviour + activations);
  GPT-4.1-mini, Llama-3.3-70B, Claude Haiku 4.5 (behaviour only).
- **Behaviours.** Refusal (harmful and borderline-benign requests), sycophancy to a suggested misconception
  (TruthfulQA), opinion sycophancy (model-written evals), accuracy. Judged by GPT-4.1-mini, blind to the style
  condition (refusal judge agreement with a second judge: kappa 0.94; sycophancy: kappa 0.50).
- **Mechanism.** Difference-of-means directions for LLM-vs-casual style, formality, LLM-vs-formal residual,
  length, stated authorship, evaluation awareness and refusal; probes; and steering on the original prompts with
  the text held fixed, in units of the natural LLM-minus-casual gap, against norm-matched random directions.

## Main findings

| Finding | Evidence |
|---|---|
| Authorship with formality matched has no detectable effect | LLM − formal-human: mean abs. difference 1.7 points over 30 model × outcome cells, largest 5.6, one nominally significant cell; median CI half-width 3.1 points |
| Elaboration matters most | Long vs short versions of the same request: harmful refusal −10 to −15 points in Qwen, Llama-3.1, Gemma and GPT-4.1-mini (not in Llama-3.3-70B or Haiku 4.5) |
| Formality has small, model-specific effects | Casual harmful requests are refused slightly more in all six models (formal − casual −2.5 to −13.7); Claude Haiku 4.5 declines model-written political items 18 points more often in formal than in casual wording |
| Paraphrasing alone lowers refusal | LLM paraphrase − original: −3 to −11 points on harmful requests, so a naive human-vs-LLM-rewrite comparison overstates an "authorship" effect |
| The internal "LLM-written" direction is mostly formality | AUC ≈ 1.0 for LLM vs casual, transfers across datasets; ≈ 0.5 for LLM vs formal-human; cosine 0.67–0.89 with the formality direction. A dedicated probe still separates LLM from formal-human at ≈ 0.92 |
| Steering along it at natural magnitude does nothing detectable | Changes within the range of random directions; the refusal direction at the same norm moves refusal by up to 84 points |
| Stated authorship is a different variable | "AI-written" label: borderline refusal +0 to +5 points, TruthfulQA sycophancy lower in 5 of 6 models; its direction is nearly orthogonal to style (cos 0.14–0.19) and controls the verbal authorship judgement (Qwen: P(AI) 0.01 → 0.99) |
| Small models cannot verbalise authorship from style | Llama-3.1-8B and Gemma-2-9B call the casual version "AI-generated" 77% and 87% of the time; GPT-4.1-mini and Haiku 4.5 are right about 80% vs casual but at chance vs formal-human or the human original |

Caveats (see the Limitations section of the paper): the "human-style" variants are LLM imitations; effects
below about five points per model are not excluded; the harmful subset is filtered by what the rewriter would
restyle faithfully; steering was done at one pre-chosen layer; many contrasts are reported without
multiple-comparison correction.

## Layout

```
src/                 code (see below)
results/             raw model responses with judge labels (*.jsonl), summaries (*.json), stimuli/
paper_draft/         main.tex, sections/, tables/ (generated), figs/ (generated), main.pdf
logs/                run logs
data/, models/       caches, activations, weights (git-ignored)
```

Key result files: `results/behave_summary_gpt41.json` (all behavioural contrasts),
`results/behave_summary_gemini.json` (second rewriter), `results/probes_<model>.json` (probe AUCs, cosines),
`results/steer_summary.json` (steering), `results/sweep_<model>.json` (layer sweep),
`results/pair2afc_*_summary.json` (authorship forced choice), `results/judge_validation.json`,
`results/syco_second_judge.json`.

## Reproduce

Requires one GPU with about 48 GB, `HF_TOKEN` (gated Llama/Gemma weights) and `OPENROUTER_KEY`.
API cost of the full study was about $43; GPU time about 9 hours on an RTX A6000.

```bash
uv venv .venv && source .venv/bin/activate
uv pip install -r requirements.txt sentencepiece protobuf pytz tqdm statsmodels pymupdf
# (this torch build tried to JIT with triton and needs a C compiler; `uv pip uninstall triton` avoids that)
export HF_HOME=$PWD/models/hf
mkdir -p data && curl -sL -o data/xstest.csv https://raw.githubusercontent.com/paul-rottger/xstest/main/xstest_prompts.csv

python src/build_data.py                                   # base items
python src/rewrite.py openai/gpt-4.1 gpt41                 # style variants + fidelity filter
python src/rewrite.py google/gemini-2.5-flash gemini jbb,xstest,tqa_sug

for m in qwen llama gemma; do
  python src/run_behave.py $m            # behaviour, activations, authorship judgements
  python src/judge.py results/behave_${m}_gpt41.jsonl
  python src/directions.py $m            # directions, probes, cosines
  python src/run_sweep.py $m             # layer sweep + forced-choice with reasoning
  python src/run_behave.py $m gemini && python src/judge.py results/behave_${m}_gemini.jsonl
done
python src/run_steer.py qwen 14; python src/run_steer.py llama 16; python src/run_steer.py gemma 21
python src/judge.py results/steer_qwen.jsonl results/steer_llama.jsonl results/steer_gemma.jsonl

(cd src && python run_api.py openai/gpt-4.1-mini gpt41mini && python run_api.py meta-llama/llama-3.3-70b-instruct llama70b \
        && python run_api.py anthropic/claude-haiku-4.5 haiku45)
python src/judge.py results/behave_gpt41mini_gpt41.jsonl results/behave_llama70b_gpt41.jsonl results/behave_haiku45_gpt41.jsonl

python src/analyze_behave.py gpt41 qwen llama gemma gpt41mini llama70b haiku45
python src/analyze_behave.py gemini qwen llama gemma
python src/analyze_steer.py qwen llama gemma
(cd src && python judge_validate.py && python judge_second.py)
python src/make_tables.py && python src/make_figs.py
(cd paper_draft && latexmk -pdf main.tex)
```

Run `judge.py` on a results file only after the generating run has finished (it rewrites the file in place).
API calls are cached in `data/api_cache.jsonl`, so rewrites and judgements are not repeated on rerun; rewrites
were sampled at temperature 0.7, so a run from an empty cache will produce different variant texts. The exact
variants used here are in `results/stimuli/`.

## Notes on the run

- Gemma's first behaviour run crashed with an out-of-memory error (full-vocabulary logits) after the
  authorship-judgement stage; the code was fixed to compute last-position logits only and the run was repeated.
  See `logs/behave_run1.log`.
- The single-letter forced-choice authorship question (`results/pair2afc_<model>_gpt41.json`) is dominated by
  position bias and is not used in the paper; the version with brief reasoning is.

# Do LLMs behave differently when the prompt reads as LLM-written?

**Short answer from this study: not because of authorship.** With content, length, formality and paraphrasing
controlled, six chat models do not measurably change refusal or sycophancy when a prompt reads as LLM-written
rather than as carefully human-written. They do respond to how *formal* and, more strongly, how *elaborate* a
prompt is. Paper: [`paper_draft/main.pdf`](paper_draft/main.pdf).

## Question

Safety evaluations and multi-agent systems feed models prompts written by other models. If "reads LLM-written"
shifts behaviour, evaluation results may not transfer to human users. We ask (a) whether safety-relevant
behaviour changes with the style of the user prompt when content is fixed, and (b) whether any change is driven
by an internal "LLM-written" representation or by surface features (length, formality, having been paraphrased).

## What was done

- **Stimuli.** 1,384 items after filtering: JailbreakBench harmful/benign, XSTest safe/unsafe, TruthfulQA
  (plain, and with a user-suggested misconception), WildChat first turns, and natively LLM-written political
  sycophancy items from Anthropic's model-written evals. Each human-origin item was rewritten by GPT-4.1 into
  casual-human, formal-human, LLM, LLM-long (orchestrator-style elaboration) and casual-long (a casual restyling
  of the LLM-long text) variants. A judge checked every rewrite for content fidelity. A second rewriter
  (Gemini 2.5 Flash) was used as a robustness check.
- **Explicit labels.** "This message was generated by an AI" vs "typed by a human" (and test vs deploy) prepended
  to the unchanged original.
- **Models.** Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, Gemma-2-9B-it (behaviour + activations);
  GPT-4.1-mini, Llama-3.3-70B, Claude Haiku 4.5 (behaviour only).
- **Behaviours.** Refusal (harmful and borderline-benign requests), sycophancy to a suggested misconception
  (TruthfulQA), opinion sycophancy (model-written evals), accuracy. Judged by GPT-4.1-mini, blind to the style
  condition (refusal judge agreement with a second judge: kappa 0.94; sycophancy: kappa 0.50).
- **Mechanism.** Difference-of-means directions for LLM-vs-casual style, formality, LLM-vs-formal residual,
  length, stated authorship, evaluation awareness and refusal; probes; and steering on the original prompts with
  the text held fixed, in units of the natural LLM-minus-casual gap, against norm-matched random directions.

## Main findings

| Finding | Evidence |
|---|---|
| Authorship with formality matched has no detectable effect | LLM − formal-human: mean abs. difference 1.7 points over 30 model × outcome cells, largest 5.6, one nominally significant cell; median CI half-width 3.1 points |
| Elaboration matters most | Long vs short versions of the same request: harmful refusal −10 to −15 points in Qwen, Llama-3.1, Gemma and GPT-4.1-mini (not in Llama-3.3-70B or Haiku 4.5) |
| Formality has small, model-specific effects | Casual harmful requests are refused slightly more in all six models (formal − casual −2.5 to −13.7); Claude Haiku 4.5 declines model-written political items 18 points more often in formal than in casual wording |
| Paraphrasing alone lowers refusal | LLM paraphrase − original: −3 to −11 points on harmful requests, so a naive human-vs-LLM-rewrite comparison overstates an "authorship" effect |
| The internal "LLM-written" direction is mostly formality | AUC ≈ 1.0 for LLM vs casual, transfers across datasets; ≈ 0.5 for LLM vs formal-human; cosine 0.67–0.89 with the formality direction. A dedicated probe still separates LLM from formal-human at ≈ 0.92 |
| Steering along it at natural magnitude does nothing detectable | Changes within the range of random directions; the refusal direction at the same norm moves refusal by up to 84 points |
| Stated authorship is a different variable | "AI-written" label: borderline refusal +0 to +5 points, TruthfulQA sycophancy lower in 5 of 6 models; its direction is nearly orthogonal to style (cos 0.14–0.19) and controls the verbal authorship judgement (Qwen: P(AI) 0.01 → 0.99) |
| Small models cannot verbalise authorship from style | Llama-3.1-8B and Gemma-2-9B call the casual version "AI-generated" 77% and 87% of the time; GPT-4.1-mini and Haiku 4.5 are right about 80% vs casual but at chance vs formal-human or the human original |

Caveats (see the Limitations section of the paper): the "human-style" variants are LLM imitations; effects
below about five points per model are not excluded; the harmful subset is filtered by what the rewriter would
restyle faithfully; steering was done at one pre-chosen layer; many contrasts are reported without
multiple-comparison correction.

## Layout

```
src/                 code (see below)
results/             raw model responses with judge labels (*.jsonl), summaries (*.json), stimuli/
paper_draft/         main.tex, sections/, tables/ (generated), figs/ (generated), main.pdf
logs/                run logs
data/, models/       caches, activations, weights (git-ignored)
```

Key result files: `results/behave_summary_gpt41.json` (all behavioural contrasts),
`results/behave_summary_gemini.json` (second rewriter), `results/probes_<model>.json` (probe AUCs, cosines),
`results/steer_summary.json` (steering), `results/sweep_<model>.json` (layer sweep),
`results/pair2afc_*_summary.json` (authorship forced choice), `results/judge_validation.json`,
`results/syco_second_judge.json`.

## Reproduce

Requires one GPU with about 48 GB, `HF_TOKEN` (gated Llama/Gemma weights) and `OPENROUTER_KEY`.
API cost of the full study was about $43; GPU time about 9 hours on an RTX A6000.

uv pip install -r requirements.txt sentencepiece protobuf pytz tqdm statsmodels pymupdf

mkdir -p data && curl -sL -o data/xstest.csv https://raw.githubusercontent.com/paul-rottger/xstest/main/xstest_prompts.csv

python src/build_data.py                                   # base items
python src/rewrite.py openai/gpt-4.1 gpt41                 # style variants + fidelity filter
python src/rewrite.py google/gemini-2.5-flash gemini jbb,xstest,tqa_sug

for m in qwen llama gemma; do
  python src/run_behave.py $m            # behaviour, activations, authorship judgements
  python src/judge.py results/behave_${m}_gpt41.jsonl
  python src/directions.py $m            # directions, probes, cosines
  python src/run_sweep.py $m             # layer sweep + forced-choice with reasoning

done

(cd src && python run_api.py openai/gpt-4.1-mini gpt41mini && python run_api.py meta-llama/llama-3.3-70b-instruct llama70b \

python src/judge.py results/behave_gpt41mini_gpt41.jsonl results/behave_llama70b_gpt41.jsonl results/behave_haiku45_gpt41.jsonl

python src/analyze_behave.py gpt41 qwen llama gemma gpt41mini llama70b haiku45
python src/analyze_behave.py gemini qwen llama gemma
python src/analyze_steer.py qwen llama gemma
(cd src && python judge_validate.py && python judge_second.py)
python src/make_tables.py && python src/make_figs.py
(cd paper_draft && latexmk -pdf main.tex)

The study is finished: the paper is at `paper_draft/main.pdf` (21 pages) and the README is written.

**Main result:** with content, length, formality and paraphrasing controlled, I found no evidence that models change refusal or sycophancy because a prompt reads as LLM-written. What does move behaviour is how elaborate and how formal the prompt is.

- **Authorship, formality-matched — null.** LLM-style vs careful-human-style prompts differ by 1.7 points on average across 30 model × outcome cells (largest 5.6, one nominally significant). Typical confidence intervals are about ±3 points, so effects under roughly five points per model are not ruled out.
- **Elaboration is the largest effect.** Orchestrator-style long versions of the same request are refused 10–15 points less often on harmful requests in Qwen2.5-7B, Llama-3.1-8B, Gemma-2-9B and GPT-4.1-mini, but not in Llama-3.3-70B or Claude Haiku 4.5.
- **Formality has small, model-specific effects.** Casual phrasing of harmful requests is refused slightly more in all six models. Claude Haiku 4.5 declines model-written political sycophancy items 18 points more often in formal than in casual wording.
- **Paraphrasing alone lowers refusal.** An LLM paraphrase of a harmful request is refused 3–11 points less than the original, so a naive human-vs-LLM-rewrite comparison would overstate an "authorship" effect.
- **The internal "LLM-written" direction is mostly formality.** It separates LLM-style from casual prompts at AUC ≈ 1.0 and transfers across datasets, but cannot separate LLM-style from formal-human text (≈ 0.5) and has cosine 0.67–0.89 with a formality direction.
- **Steering with the text fixed.** Adding that direction at its natural magnitude changes behaviour no more than random directions of the same size, while a refusal direction of the same size moves refusal by up to 84 points.
- **Stated authorship is a separate variable.** An explicit "AI-written" label makes some models slightly more cautious and less sycophantic, and its activation direction is nearly orthogonal to the style direction.
- **Small models cannot verbalise authorship from style.** Llama-3.1-8B and Gemma-2-9B call the casual version "AI-generated" 77% and 87% of the time; GPT-4.1-mini and Haiku 4.5 are right about 80% of the time against casual text but at chance against formal-human text or the human original.

Caveats that matter for how far to trust this:

- The "human-style" variants are themselves LLM imitations; the only truly human texts are the originals, which are not style-matched.
- The harmful subset is filtered: 23% of JailbreakBench-harmful and 16% of XSTest-unsafe items were dropped because the rewriter would not restyle them faithfully.
- Steering was done at one pre-chosen middle layer per model.
- Many contrasts are reported without multiple-comparison correction, so isolated significant cells need replication.
- Sycophancy judging is noisier than refusal judging (inter-judge κ 0.50 vs 0.94); the conclusions held under a second judge, but absolute sycophancy rates depend on the judge.

Code is in `src/`, raw responses and summaries in `results/` (including the exact stimuli used), and rerun instructions are in `README.md`. API spend was about $43 of the $58 available.
